vignette: Kwame was a 20-year-old African man who had come to the clinic after months of feeling as though something in him had broken and not returned. A single, unmarried doctor, he had prided himself on being calm under pressure, the kind of person patients and coworkers could look to in an emergency. That certainty began to unravel during a combat deployment when his unit came under fire and the air around him changed all at once: gunshots, people shouting, and then the terrifying, unnatural silence that followed when the firing stopped and he could hear his own breathing. He later described that breathing as sharp and labored, as if his chest had forgotten how to work. In the aftermath, those moments returned to him not as a full story but in disconnected pieces that would flash up and then slip away. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, and there were stretches he simply could not reconstruct no matter how hard he tried. Each time the memory broke through in fragments, it brought a harsh conclusion with it: that he had not been strong enough, and that this must mean something was wrong with him now. The image of the attack made those beliefs feel less like fears than facts. Since coming home, Kwame had become convinced that the attack had done more than frighten him. It had destroyed the assumptions he had lived by. Because he had come to see himself as permanently changed and on guard, almost anything could turn into a reminder - a raised voice in the hospital corridor, the wrong kind of silence after a room emptied, or the feel of his own breathing turning shallow on a rushed shift. Those moments did not just startle him; they seemed to confirm his belief that he was now the kind of man who had to scan for threat everywhere. Once he settled on that conclusion, ordinary cues began to feel loaded with meaning: a silence in a corridor or a sudden pause in conversation no longer seemed neutral, but like proof that danger could return without warning. Each reminder fed the same belief that the world was unsafe and that he could not trust his own sense of when things were about to go wrong. He spoke with a quiet bitterness about no longer knowing himself, as if the man who had once wanted to heal people and trust his own judgment had been replaced by someone unfamiliar and permanently altered. What unsettled him most was that ordinary life no longer felt ordinary: sudden silence in a corridor, the pause after a conversation stops, or the sensation of being short of breath during a rushed hospital shift could send him back into the feeling that danger was near. Violence on a television screen or even a heated argument nearby sharpened that sense immediately. Each of these moments seemed to confirm his belief that the world did not work the way he had been taught, and that he had to stay on guard all the time because safety could vanish without warning. That way of thinking made the memories harder to face. When images or fragments rose up, he would clamp down on them before they became too clear, afraid that if he let the scene come into focus he would be overwhelmed by what it meant about him and about the world. The more he tried to keep the belief at bay, the more the memory seemed to push back into view, as if the mind kept returning him to the moment in order to prove how deeply it had changed him. When the scene came back, it carried the same conviction with it: that something in him had been permanently altered by what happened. He noticed that the more he tried not to remember, the more the event returned in broken pieces: a flash of dust, the pressure in his chest, the instant of silence after the violence, and then blankness. Those gaps only deepened his sense that something essential was missing, and that he was perhaps missing part of himself with it. In that state, he became even more alert to anything that could hint at threat. He watched faces, listened for changes in tone, and especially reacted to breathlessness in his own body, interpreting it as a sign that danger was close or that he was losing control again. At work, these moments had begun to intrude into the practical rhythm of being a doctor. During long shifts, when a patient room suddenly went quiet or when he felt himself needing to catch his breath, the old fear returned with enough force that he would excuse himself, step into the hallway, and stand listening for sounds that reassured him. He avoided unnecessary exposure to violence in news reports and shrank away from conversations about conflict, but he could not avoid the hospital environment, where emergencies and silence could appear without warning. Over weeks, that constant watchfulness and the effort to keep the memory at bay left him more exhausted and less certain of his place among colleagues. He said he had started to feel as if he was acting the part of a doctor rather than being one, because the confidence he used to trust no longer felt like his own. By the time he sought help, Kwame was frightened less by the original event than by the way it kept organizing his present. He was afraid he would keep losing pieces of the memory, and with them whatever was left of his identity, but he was also afraid that if he remembered too much he would be unable to bear what it said about the world. Those fragments were enough to make him begin noticing echoes of the event in the present, as if the memory itself had taught him where to look for danger. A sudden hush in a patient room or the sound of his own breath catching could pull his attention there at once, and he would move through the rest of the shift as though those cues were warnings he could not afford to ignore. He came in hoping to understand why silence and breathlessness had become so powerful, and whether he could ever feel like himself again without always having to stand guard.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph clearly shows triggers/reminders causing negative appraisals; the cues are described as increasing threat and alertness, but not as leading to negative beliefs or appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph states that negative appraisals drive the traumatic memory to return or intensify.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph shows negative appraisals causing triggers or reminders to arise.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph explicitly shows the traumatic memory leading to negative appraisals; the vignette links memory fragments to fear and threat, but not to beliefs about self or world.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph explicitly shows the traumatic memory causing triggers/reminders; the cues are presented as eliciting threat, but not as being produced by the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
